blocks.text: I died on the hardwood floor at my husband’s birthday dinner, and my three-year-old was the only person who stayed beside me.

I didn’t understand that right away. At first I was trying to get up. I could see the cake, the chairs, Wyatt’s guests looking down at me, and I remember thinking my hair was going to be full of crumbs.
Then I saw Piper kneeling by my arm, and I couldn’t make my hand move toward her. That was when I knew something was badly wrong.

There had been little things before the fall. I kept telling myself not to make a big deal out of them. Wyatt’s phone turned face down whenever Harper came into the room. He and Harper had been close since college, and Wyatt said I was making trouble by asking why she texted him after midnight. Brenda, his mother, told me not to “pick at a good thing.” I was tired of being the difficult one, so I let it go.

Wyatt’s birthday dinner was at our house. We had a long dining table and a lot of people, though I can’t tell you now exactly who all was there. I remember the blue frosting on the cake because Piper got it on her sleeve.
I remember Wyatt laughing too loud at something Harper said. I remember that I had saved him the chair by the window because he always said he liked sitting there.

That chair mattered to me for a silly reason. Piper had started dragging her little wooden chair around the house and parking it beside mine. She’d say it was our place. Wyatt used to laugh when she did that. He didn’t laugh that night.

Harper had been at my shoulder for most of dinner. She wore the easy smile she used whenever Wyatt was watching. I knew about the affair by then. Not every detail, but enough. I had found a hotel charge on a card statement and a message that said, “Same room as last time.” Wyatt told me it was a work mix-up. I wanted to believe him, or maybe I wanted not to have to decide what to do next.

When dinner ended, I stood with Piper on my hip and reached for the chair by the window. I was tired, and my feet hurt. Harper moved behind me. I saw her hand on the chair back, but I thought she was just making room.

I fell hard. My head struck the floor. There was a sharp crack, and the small barrette in my hair broke beneath me. I heard the guests laugh before I could make sense of the pain. Or maybe it was after. I can’t place the order now. I know I heard them.
Harper looked down at me and said, “Well, that was elegant.” Somebody laughed again. Then Harper added, “Maybe she should practice sitting down a little more.”
Piper slid off my lap and landed beside me. She was crying, but she didn’t run. “Mommy, get up,” she said. I tried to tell her I was there. I tried to move my mouth. Nothing came out.
Wyatt looked at me, then looked at his guests. “Don’t start,” he said. “You’re being dramatic.”

I’d heard him say that before, usually when I asked a question he didn’t want to answer. This time I could see his shoes from the floor. I could see him standing there while I couldn’t lift my head. Brenda sighed and said, “Corinne, honestly. You’ve done this kind of thing before.”
I hadn’t. Not once. I’d never fallen down at dinner or faked an injury. But I couldn’t correct her. I couldn’t even call Piper’s name.

The room kept moving around me. A guest picked up a dropped napkin. Someone poured more wine. I saw Harper lean close to Wyatt and whisper something I couldn’t hear. He glanced down at me again, and then turned away.

I understood in pieces. The floor was still there under my cheek, but I wasn’t feeling it anymore. I could see my own body below me, and I couldn’t reach it. I was dead. I don’t have a better way to put it.

Piper stayed. She sat on the floor beside my body and touched my sleeve. I wanted to tell her that she hadn’t done anything wrong. I wanted to say her name, even once, so she’d know I was still with her. I couldn’t touch her. I couldn’t make a sound.

A little later, she found her wooden chair. I watched her drag it across the room. One leg caught in the rug, and she had to pull twice. She got it beside me and tried to push it close enough for my hand to reach. Then she leaned over the chair and whispered, “Here, Mommy. I’ll keep it steady for you. Now you can sit down.”
That was the line I kept with me. Not because it was clever or because she understood what had happened. She was three. She thought I needed somewhere to sit.

Hours went by. I don’t know how long. People came and went, but nobody came close enough to help me. Wyatt and Harper stayed in the dining room after the guests left. Their voices were lower then. I could hear the ice shifting in a glass and the soft scrape of a chair.
Wyatt said, “She’s breathing, probably.”
I was not breathing. I wanted to scream that at him. Instead I watched him set his glass down and look at the place where I lay.
“We can’t have police in here over this,” he said. “Not with everyone here.”

They knew I wasn’t getting up. They knew enough to be worried. But they were more worried about what might come out if anyone asked questions. Harper had pulled my chair away on purpose. Wyatt knew she and I had fought, and he knew the cameras in the dining room recorded the table.
At some point, they fetched a light blanket and tossed it over me. It didn’t cover my feet. Harper said, “There. That’s better.” Wyatt answered, “We’ll deal with it in the morning.”

Piper stayed on the floor. She had fallen asleep with her cheek on the seat of her little chair. I could not move the blanket off myself. I could not pull it up over her. I could only stay close and watch.

The next morning, Wyatt’s brother Lucas arrived early. He was due for a family business meeting, an audit he’d been asking Wyatt to let him do for months. Wyatt didn’t like Lucas asking questions. They’d been on bad terms for a while, though I never knew all of it. Lucas had been quiet at dinner, watching more than he talked.

He came through the front door at . I know the time because his phone lit up when he checked it. He called for Wyatt, got no answer, then walked toward the dining room. The house was too quiet. Piper was still on the floor beside me, and the blanket looked like something somebody had thrown down in a hurry.
Lucas stopped. “Piper,” he said softly. “What happened?”
She looked at him and rubbed her eyes. “Mommy fell.”
He moved toward the blanket. I wanted to warn him. I wanted to tell him not to lift it, though I knew he had to see.
He saw my face, then the broken barrette near my head. He reached down and pressed two fingers to my neck. After a few seconds he pulled back. He looked at my head again and didn’t touch me.
Piper came closer, and Lucas put an arm out to keep her from reaching for me. He did it gently. I was grateful for that.
“Call 911,” he told the housekeeper, who had just come in from the kitchen. Then he turned toward the stairs and shouted Wyatt’s name.
Wyatt came down in yesterday’s shirt. Harper was behind him. Brenda followed, buttoning her robe. Wyatt took one look at Lucas kneeling beside me and said, “She’s fine. She’s been doing this.”
Wyatt started to say something else, but Lucas cut him off. “I checked her pulse. Call the police.”

Harper looked at the blanket and then at Wyatt. It was a quick look, but Lucas saw it. I saw it too. Lucas asked why nobody had called for help the night before. Wyatt said he’d thought I was sleeping it off. Harper said she had gone upstairs early.
Neither answer fit the room. Piper was there. The broken chair was there. So was the blanket.

Lucas knew the security system was tied to the home server. He’d helped Wyatt set it up years before, back when they still trusted each other. He went to the office and pulled up the dining room footage. Wyatt followed him, telling him to shut it off. Lucas didn’t.

The camera showed Harper stand behind my chair. It showed her look toward Wyatt before she pulled it away. It showed me fall and strike my head. It showed Wyatt look at me and then turn back to his guests.
The footage kept going after the guests left. It showed Harper and Wyatt standing over me. It showed them talking. It showed the blanket.

Lucas played it again for the officers when they arrived. I could see the small screen reflected in his glasses. Wyatt tried to say Harper was joking. Harper said she hadn’t meant for me to fall so hard. But there it was, clear as anything. The chair moved because Harper pulled it.

The medical examiner later confirmed I’d died from a skull fracture at the dinner, from the impact to the back of my head. There was no waking up in the morning. No fainting. No chance that I could have stood up if somebody had just waited longer.

The police arrested Harper for the assault that caused my death. Wyatt was taken in over his part in leaving me there and trying to cover it up. His money didn’t make the footage disappear. The court froze the family assets while the criminal case moved forward, and the house was no longer his to run like nothing had happened.

Brenda tried to explain herself. She said she thought I was being dramatic because that was what Wyatt told her. She said she didn’t know I was dead. I watched Lucas look at her and ask, “Did you check?”

Lucas stayed with Piper. He got emergency custody while the case went on, and he made sure she didn’t have to return to that house. He brought her to his place, where she had a room and a little table for drawing. Piper didn’t understand why I wasn’t coming. Lucas didn’t lie to her. He told her I had died and that she was safe with him.
I stayed close until I saw that she believed him.

A few days later, I watched Lucas set Piper’s small wooden chair beside the window in his living room. Morning sun fell across the seat. Piper sat nearby, holding a new toy, and smiled up at her uncle. Lucas smiled back, but he kept one hand on the chair so it wouldn’t tip.
I had wanted somebody to keep it steady.
